title: Caring for Hungry Ghosts
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: The talk's main teaching is that all beings are interconnected and suffering, including those who have passed away or are struggling with internal difficulties. The ceremony aims to acknowledge this suffering by offering peace, forgiveness, and teachings to "hungry ghosts" - beings consumed by desire and desperation - particularly through the power of sound. By participating in the ceremony, individuals can cultivate a sense of compassion and connection with all beings, including those who have passed away, and experience spiritual renewal and healing.

That's how often the turtle needs to get air.
So it pokes its head up to get air, and once in a very rare while, it'll happen on its hundredth-year breath to poke its head up through this floating wooden yoke.
That's how likely it is you'll be born as a human.
It's as likely as that.
So we don't always appreciate it fully, I think.
But we might also be born as an animal, which in Buddhist cosmology is a little less positive than in modern ecology.
I think it'd be neat to be an animal.
But Buddhism says, well, you're just so consumed with eating and not being eaten, and you can't really practice.
And below that is the realm that we're talking about tonight, the realm of the hungry ghost.
The beings in this realm are sort of in between in every way.
They sort of have bodies and they sort of don't.
You can't usually see them.
Some people can sense their presence.
And they're really desperate.
It's a desperate realm.
The hungry ghosts want, want, want.
They're just consumed by desire.
Sometimes they're depicted as literally hungry: starved, famine-stricken.
And they have huge bellies, but they have these pencil-thin necks and they can't get any food down.
So our idea tonight is both a literal idea, and in Buddhism this is a very literal, real thing, as far as I can figure out.
In every world system and in this very room, usually in the corners, I understand, they kind of hide out in the corners.
They're hungry ghosts right now.
And they're vanished, and they're desperate and upset and frightened.
So our ceremony tonight is to offer them a little peace, to offer them food, to give them beautiful offerings of teachings and sound.
They especially relate to sound, it turns out.
Other senses not so good, but they can hear.
So in the ceremony we'll call them forward with sound and then we'll try to take care of them the best we can.
I want to read a short essay here from one of the teachers I got to work with a little bit, about this ceremony.
His name is, was, Kyogen Carlson.
He died very suddenly five, six years ago.
And I don't think he's a hungry ghost.
I think he lived a wonderful life.
But in the ceremony we also consider people we know who have passed, who may be wandering in these realms, desperate.
And in the ceremony we can also consider the qualities within us that are that way.
We all have these qualities, right?
So let's hear how Kyogen explains that.
It's not very long.
I'll say another thing or two and then we'll go ahead and do the ceremony.
It's an interesting thing to hold.
I feel moved to say another thing before I read this.
On the one hand, it's fun.
It's festive.
We can dress up.
Some people are modeling so beautifully.
It's great looking up over there.
It's great looking up in general.
But it's also very serious.
There's a lot of suffering, right?
It's touching into the depth and desperation of suffering.
So we feel both strong and capable and generous, able to heal ourselves and heal the whole world on the one hand, and have fun doing it too.
Healing the world doesn't have to be big drudgery.
It could be really fun.
But also we shouldn't lose sight or felt sense that we're pretty desperate.
And times are desperate.
And the hungry ghosts, wherever they are, within us and without us, are really in bad shape.
This ceremony used to have the Japanese name Segaki, which is the name that he's going to use in this essay.
Se is to feed or offer and Gaki is the Japanese word for hungry ghosts.
They're called Preta in Sanskrit and Pali.
But at some point there was a weird thing that happened in Japan, and I came in on the middle of the story.
I never quite understood what happened.
Maybe later somebody can tell me if they know.
This idea of hungry ghosts was being used in a really violent and negative way in Japanese culture.
And the Soto Church Central, Soto-shu, said we're not going to call it Segaki anymore.
We call it Seijiki.
And we decided to just not worry about that because we're not Japanese.
It was being used as such a raggedy term for minority.
Yeah.
And not in Japan.
So it was considered racist.
Thank you.
Yeah, that was something like that.
Thanks.
Thanks Rishi.
Yeah, exactly.
So we wouldn't want to be doing something that somehow got a racist tone to it.
So we can call it spirit-settling or feeding the hungry ghosts.
So here's what Kyogen Roshi said.
*The name Segaki means feeding the hungry ghosts.
And the festival contains a great deal of teaching about training and Buddhism.
On the one hand, it is a time of remembering the dead and resolving our karmic connections with those who have died.
It is also a time to resolve our own internal karmic difficulties and for letting go of the obstacles and blockages we carry with us.
The festival is said to have begun when Moggallana, a disciple of the Buddha, was plagued by dreams of his recently departed mother suffering in a world in which she could neither eat nor drink.
Food would turn to fire and water would turn to blood or pus whenever it touched her mouth.*
*Moggallana went to the Buddha and told him about his dreams, which plagued him every night.
And the Buddha explained that he was seeing the suffering of his mother in the world of the Gaki, the world of the hungry ghosts.
Gaki are usually depicted having long skinny necks with throats much too small for swallowing and bloated bulging stomachs common to severe malnutrition.
This imagery is a fantastic description of a spiritual state that can be seen every day right here in this physical world of women and men.
A condition which everyone suffers from and has suffered from to one degree or another at some point in his or her life.*
*On the most spiritual level it is the state of someone desperately wanting to know the truth who cannot accept the teachings.
She knows that she is suffering and the religious practice will help but he cannot stop resisting and holding on to his personal opinions and ego.
He goes to drink the Dharma but his throat will not accept it.
Every time she rejects the teaching it turns into fire in her mouth.

On a personal level, everyday level, it is the condition of someone who desperately needs but like a person with a phantom itch can find no relief in many ways that we endlessly turn and suffer and desire.
Too often our attempts to attain the things we want turn us in this way, turn us into hungry ghosts.*

*Moggallana's dreams were due to his deep connection with his mother and the Buddha's advice to him was that he make offerings to her of whatever food that she could most easily accept and digest and that this would be done in a ceremony dedicated in her name at the time when the monks conducted their regular gatherings to confess their transgressions, precept ceremony.
This is where the connection between making offerings to the dead and the cleansing of karma personal or in connection with someone who has died becomes apparent.
Today the tradition that started with this ceremony is continued every year in Buddhist temples by making an offering on a table away from the statue or pictures of the Buddha or Bodhisattva.
For those who reject religious teaching it's a kindness to offer without doctrine that this is actually the true religious act.*
So that's why we made a special altar over there away from the Buddha.
The Buddha can kind of look on in the distance and see how it's going.
*For the Dharma to be truly Dharma it can only be offered in forms that can be accepted and made use of.
Offerings of any type made in such a manner will naturally benefit the recipient and the donor.
This principle applies to so many situations we encounter in everyday life.
Such action naturally expresses all acceptance in a way that touches and deeply affects all concerned.
Hungry ghosts are not the only ones to be remembered at Segaki, however.
It's a time to remember all who have died and be thankful for their having lived and give thanks to the teachings that their lives gave to us.*

*Because it's a time for us to let go of our clinging to those who have died and realize that their training goes on in whatever form it now takes and they do not need us pulling them back into the world through our attachment.
By letting go of those who are gone we can also resolve any painful memories that linger on in us that become the nucleus of a multitude of other problems.
All acceptance is the key.
If we can completely accept those who have gone as they were we can understand them better and offer them what they need to go on which is most often our forgiveness, our blessing.
If you apply this process to yourself too, looking at your own past actions at what must be let go of, it's easy to see the connection between Segaki and personal karmic cleansing.
It becomes a time of deep personal spiritual renewal.*
*In the way we are adapting Buddhist tradition to our culture Segaki is celebrated in or near Halloween Day.
In Western culture Halloween, and All Souls Day, All Saints Day, El Dia de los Muertos is celebrated when the ghosts and goblins from the past come out of hiding.
What better time to offer them merit and put them back to rest.
The themes of death, change and spiritual transition have for centuries in the West been remembered in the autumn at the time of change from light to dark, from hot to cold.
Although in the Far East Segaki is celebrated mid-summer.
Within that culture that is a time similar to Halloween in our own.
The summer solstice is a time of transition just as the autumn equinox is for us, both representing a time of change when the past can be left behind, a new beginning is possible.
Segaki, hungry ghosts, is a celebration of how this works on every level.*
Ohana will tell us a little bit, once we are up in action, about the flow in the room, but I just want to mention a few things about the actual ceremony.
It is a very participatory thing.
We are all fully a part of it.

We are going to make some noise together to invite them here so they will feel comfortable, and then we will give them the offerings that we put on the table, including different kinds of food and other tokens of our feelings that people put there.
This is the first time we have done this in many years, so [unclear: "if you are now feeling like we are going to do it in different ways that we connect to this ceremony"].
The best offering we can give them is the offering of good teachings.
We will do a chant that we don't usually do called the Gate of Sweet Dew, and you will see what that is when we chant it.

And we will offer them the Daihishin Dharani, that is kind of a magical spell that warms up compassion, and it is wonderfully un-understandable, so it is a good thing to transmit between worlds because it is not hampered by our thinking we know what it means.
There will be a dedication as usual.
Kokyo will make a dedication, but what I am getting to is, in the middle of that dedication, if you like, what would you like to offer this ceremony to?
An appreciation for someone who has passed, or in hopes that wherever they are they are well?
Do you want to offer this ceremony to your own clinging or fear or shame?
You could name that.
You could name "my dear brother" or "my desperate desire," whatever arises for you, or you can just be quiet and offer your breath and your body.
In many ways it is like any other Zen ceremony, but our orientation is kind of the other way.
And we will do some singing.
We will offer them music, which is a modern addition.

One of my colleagues and teachers, Bernie Glassman, felt like it would be great to have something we could really sing in English, and so he asked the great kirtan singer Krishna Das to write something, which he did.
Also, like many of our great spiritual leaders, he is a Jewish guy from the Bronx.
And they don't like it if you are from Brooklyn, you don't like it if they say it from the Bronx.
I never keep it straight, so I am probably going to get in trouble.
Peter is from the Bronx.
I said Brooklyn one time.
He [unclear: "has rapes"].
So we will have that in there too, and offer him singing our voices as best we can.
Thank you.
